title: David's Charge and the Plan for the Temple
summary: David gathers all the leaders of Israel in Jerusalem and tells them that God refused him the building of the temple but chose Solomon to build it and to sit on the LORD's throne. He charges the assembly and Solomon to seek and obey God, then hands Solomon the written plan for the temple, its rooms, its service, and its furnishings, and urges him to be strong and carry out the work.
story: After the long lists of chapters 23 to 27, the story resumes with a public ceremony. The officials who were just organized are now summoned together, and David, old and near the end of his reign, speaks to them as a father and a king. This is a transfer of power and of purpose. First Chronicles has been moving toward the temple since David brought the ark to Jerusalem (chapters 13 to 16) and received God's promise that his son would build a house (chapter 17). Here that promise is passed into Solomon's hands in front of the nation, and the next chapter will complete the handover with gifts, prayer, and Solomon's anointing.
historical:
The scene belongs to the last years of David's reign, around 970 BC. First Kings 1 tells the succession very differently, as a tense palace struggle in which Adonijah, David's older son, tried to seize the throne and Nathan and Bathsheba moved David to name Solomon. Chronicles leaves that intrigue out and presents a calm, public commissioning. The two accounts are not necessarily in conflict; the Chronicler knew his readers had Kings, and he chose to show the side of the succession that concerned the temple and the nation's covenant with God.

The first readers of Chronicles, living in Persian-period Judah after the return from exile, worshiped in a rebuilt temple that was modest compared with Solomon's. Hearing that the first temple was built from a God-given plan and served by divisions of priests and Levites organized by David himself gave their own worship a pedigree. They were not inventing religion; they were continuing what God had given.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, temples were understood as the dwelling places of gods, often built by kings as a sign of divine favor on their reign. David describes the temple as a resting place for the ark and a footstool for God. The ark of the covenant, a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, was imagined as the footstool of the invisible God who was enthroned above the cherubim, the winged guardian figures on its cover. The temple would not contain God; it would be the place where his feet, as it were, touched the earth.

David's detailed instructions on the weight of gold and silver for each object reflect how ancient people valued metals: by weight, not by coin. The long list of lampstands, tables for the bread of the Presence (showbread, twelve loaves set before God each week), bowls, and the incense altar echoes the tabernacle furnishings of Exodus 25 to 30. The "chariot" of the cherubim (verse 18) is a striking phrase that pictures the ark and its cherubim as God's throne-chariot, an image Ezekiel later saw in motion (Ezekiel 1 and 10).
literary: The chapter is built around two speeches with a list between them. David's first speech (verses 2 to 10) moves from the assembly to Solomon: his own desire, God's refusal, God's choosing of Judah, David, and Solomon, then the charge to keep the commandments and to seek God. The central section (11 to 19) is a catalog of the plan, repeating the word "weight" again and again. The second speech (20 and 21) returns to Solomon with words that echo Moses' charge to Joshua: “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Do not be afraid or discouraged” (compare Deuteronomy 31:7-8 and Joshua 1:6-9). The Chronicler frames the handover from David to Solomon like the handover from Moses to Joshua, from a leader who could not finish to one who would.

outline.t: David assembles the leaders of Israel
God's refusal of David and choice of Solomon
The charge to Israel and to Solomon
The plan for the temple and its furnishings

doctrines.note: David traces everything to God's choosing: Judah among the tribes, his father's house, David himself, and Solomon among many sons. The throne is called “the throne of the kingdom of the LORD” (verse 5). Israel's king rules on God's behalf, not in his own right.

God's promise to establish Solomon's kingdom forever comes with a condition: “if he resolutely carries out My commandments and ordinances” (verse 7). The Chronicler holds God's lasting promise to David's house together with the obedience required of each king.

The temple is not David's design but a plan the LORD made clear “in writing by His hand upon me” (verse 19), as the tabernacle followed the pattern shown to Moses. The place where God meets his people is shaped by God, not by human taste.
David's charge rests on a promise: God will neither fail nor forsake Solomon until the work is finished (verse 20). Courage here is not self-confidence but trust in God's presence.

words.note: Tavnit, pattern, plan, or model. It is the word used when God shows Moses the pattern of the tabernacle on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 40). By using it for David's temple plan, the Chronicler places David alongside Moses as the one through whom God gave the design for Israel's worship.

Darash, to seek, inquire, or search out. It is one of the key words of Chronicles. David urges the people to “keep and seek out all the commandments” (verse 8) and tells Solomon, “If you seek Him, He will be found by you” (verse 9). To seek God is to turn toward him with the whole life, and Chronicles measures its kings by it.

Azav, to leave, abandon, or forsake, the opposite of seeking. David warns that if Solomon forsakes God he will be rejected (verse 9), then promises that God will not forsake Solomon (verse 20). The same verb frames both the warning and the comfort.

Hadom, footstool. It appears in poetry for the ark or the temple as the place of God's feet (Psalm 99:5; 132:7) and for the earth itself (Isaiah 66:1). The image keeps God's greatness in view: even the temple is only where he rests his feet.

christ: God's words about Solomon, “I have chosen him as My son, and I will be his Father” (verse 6), repeat the promise of 2 Samuel 7:14 and 1 Chronicles 17:13. The letter to the Hebrews applies that promise to Jesus as the Son greater than the angels (Hebrews 1:5). Solomon was a son of David who built a house and ruled on the LORD's throne, but his kingdom did not last forever, because he did not keep the condition of verse 7. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David who fulfills the promise without failing its terms. The word "pattern" also carries forward: Hebrews describes the earthly sanctuary as a copy and shadow of the heavenly one, built by the pattern shown to Moses (Hebrews 8:5), and says Christ entered the true sanctuary. And the charge to be strong because God will not forsake you finds its fullest form in Jesus' promise to be with his people always (Matthew 28:20).

hard.q: Why was David, whom God helped to win his wars, disqualified from building the temple because he shed blood?
hard.a:
Verse 3, like 1 Chronicles 22:8, says David could not build God's house because he was a man of war who had spilled blood. Readers find this puzzling, since the Chronicler presents David's wars as fought with God's help. 2 Samuel 7 gives no reason at all, and 1 Kings 5:3 says David was too occupied with wars on every side.

Most interpreters don't read verse 3 as a moral condemnation of David's battles. They see a symbolic fitness: the temple was to be a house of rest and peace, and the one who built it should be a man of rest. 1 Chronicles 22:9 makes the connection explicit by linking Solomon's name with shalom, peace. Others add that a warrior's contact with death made him an unsuitable builder of the holy house, in the way Israel's law kept death away from holy things. Still others emphasize God's freedom: he gives different callings to different servants, and David's was to prepare what another would build. These readings can stand together. What the text does not say is that David's wars were sinful in themselves.

questions: David wanted to build the temple but was told no, and he spent his remaining years preparing for someone else to do it. How do you respond when God gives you a part of a work you will not see finished?
David says the LORD “searches every heart and understands the intent of every thought” (verse 9). How does that change what it means to serve God with a willing mind?
Solomon is told to be strong not because he is capable but because God is with him. Where do you need that kind of courage right now?
